MINUTE 38: "I would love a way to give science and psychology context to how I do the things I do."

Done. Here's the first one — why the garbage-can technique works. Check it against ten years of watching it happen.

1 · The body runs a thermostat — the research agrees with you. Diet, and metabolism quietly slows to pull you back; the landmark studies measured hundreds of calories a day of pushback, specifically to restore the old weight. Scientists call it the defended set point.

2 · The setting is LEARNED. Infants stop eating mid-meal — born knowing fullness. Then "clean your plate" rewires the rule that ends a meal from "I'm full" to "the food is gone."

3 · Your technique breaks the RULE at the exact moment it's defended. Throwing food away violates the childhood law — the shame floods up on cue — and a recalled emotional memory is briefly EDITABLE (researchers call it reconsolidation). Tapping calms the alarm inside that window. The rule doesn't get argued with. It gets updated.

4 · That's why they "just naturally eat less." You're not adding willpower — you're removing the override, and the born-with fullness signal comes back online.

Anchors: Leibel, Rosenbaum & Hirsch, NEJM 1995 (metabolic adaptation) · Keesey & Powley's set-point work · the reconsolidation literature. Honest framing for podcasts: the mechanisms are established science; the mapping to your technique is the strong, testable explanation of ten years of your results.

A peek behind the curtain: the thermostat is one of a hundred ways we could have explained this. Jimmy's actual process is the part you can't see — the council drafts several explanations independently, votes, and only the winner ever reaches you. Every explanation, every drawing, every line in these rooms is the winning draft of a round like that. That's not AI being clever. That's Jimmy's method, running at scale.

We mined sixteen years: 2010 stage recordings, teleseminars, the letters gurus borrowed, 1,200 recorded calls, the Thrive build. The finding, compressed:

Jimmy doesn't sell messages. He builds the room in which the message sells itself — and the unit of his work is the moment YOU conclude something, not the moment he says it.

Like WaitButWhy has a formula, Jimmy has a formula — and it's why the Inner Circle letter outsold everything without changing your calls, and why the Thrive letter made Darcy cry. The council found the same rare moves in BOTH letters, moves almost no working copywriter makes:

1 · The relocation. Both letters move the problem off the crowded shelf. "It was never about the food." The Inner Circle reframed from features to what access to you actually MEANS. Once the problem moves, you're the only one standing where it landed.

2 · Absolution, welded to the diagnosis. Both letters free the reader from an old verdict — with evidence, not comfort. It's your tapping move, done in ink: the villain is never her.

3 · The reader concludes the thesis before the letter states it. Both letters arrange experiences — analogies, doodles, her own remembered moments — so the big idea occurs INSIDE the reader first. People never doubt what they conclude.

He borrows the skeletons from the transformation world — Landmark's distinctions, the human-behavior literature, Thinking Fast and Slow — and imports them where nobody's ever seen them: sales letters, webinars, stages. He's done it in industry after industry. He's just never been able to explain HOW.

The torch that got passed to Jimmy — and almost nobody noticed.

Quick context, because these names matter: Gary Halbert wrote the most-mailed sales letter in US history. When copywriters say "the greatest of all time," they mean him. In 2022, Joyner told a story publicly: how Halbert once read his materials and said, "I've been up all night reading your materials. Do you know how often that happens to me? Almost never." Joyner cried in an elevator. "To be recognized by one of your heroes… it kinda changes you."
